strengths: Novel and timely conceptual framing: the paper reframes the Rashomon set itself as a policy/governance object and systematically studies how model multiplicity affects robustness, stability, and privacy jointly, rather than studying these properties in isolation as prior work has done.

Strong theory-to-experiment coherence: each major theoretical claim (Theorems 1-6, Corollaries 1-2, plus appendix Theorems 7-9) is paired with a corresponding empirical study, and the results are mutually consistent across six datasets (Adult, Bank, COMPAS, Credit, Diabetes, FICO), which strengthens the credibility of the central robustness-privacy trade-off claim.

The theoretical toolkit is diverse and appropriately matched to the hypothesis classes considered: counting/entropy arguments for mutual information (Theorem 1), a combinatorial argument for rule-list vulnerability (Theorem 2), Hamming-distance/triangle-inequality and margin-based arguments for reactive robustness (Section 5.1), Pinsker-based distribution shift stability (Theorem 4), and a clean chi-squared-based KL bound for ensemble leakage (Theorem 6).

Extensive and transparent experimental reporting, including detailed dataset/hyperparameter tables, multiple ensemble-construction strategies (closest/farthest/incremental/sparsest/densest), sensitivity analyses in the appendix, and an honest discussion of a candidate 'sweet spot' regime, which supports reproducibility and shows the authors probed robustness of their own findings.

The paper is clearly written, well organized with a helpful summary table (Table 1), and provides concrete, actionable policy implications (set-level governance, disclosure of representative models rather than full sets) that connect the theoretical work to real institutional practice.
weaknesses: Some core theoretical results are relatively elementary applications of standard tools (triangle inequality for Eq. 1, Pinsker's inequality for Theorem 4, Chernoff bound for Theorem 8, chi-squared KL bound for Theorem 6), so the technical novelty is modest; the contribution is primarily in the synthesis and framing rather than in new proof techniques.

The empirical privacy measure (DRAFT dataset reconstruction attack) targets a rather different notion of leakage than the theoretical mutual-information/KL bounds (Theorems 1 and 6), and DRAFT itself is only feasible on very small training sets (100 points, up to ~200 trees), raising concerns about how well the empirical trends generalize to realistic dataset sizes and richer model classes.

The notion of 'diversity' is defined inconsistently across sections (Hamming distance of classification patterns for trees, angle between weight vectors for linear models, no single unifying formalism), which makes it harder to compare robustness-privacy trade-offs across model classes or to give practitioners a single actionable diversity metric.

The adversarial threat models used empirically are fairly narrow (single-feature L0 flips with small budget, or exhaustive white-box tree evasion), and it is unclear how the reactive-robustness story would hold up against stronger, more realistic attacks or adaptive adversaries who are aware that a Rashomon set (rather than a single model) is being defended.

Several theoretical results rely on fairly strong or special-case assumptions (e.g., Theorem 2 requires majority-vote rule lists and unit L0 perturbations on binary features; Theorem 1 gives only an O(l_f log d) upper bound rather than a tight characterization), which limits how far the 'sparse models are private but fragile' narrative can be generalized beyond the specific illustrative settings chosen.

There is no comparison against alternative or complementary defenses (e.g., standard differentially private training, adversarial training, or existing moving-target defenses) to contextualize how large the reactive-robustness or privacy-leakage effects are relative to established baselines, making the practical significance of the trade-off somewhat difficult to calibrate.

The policy/governance recommendations in the conclusion (e.g., disclosing 'representative models or summary statistics') remain largely qualitative and are not backed by a formal disclosure mechanism or utility-privacy-robustness optimization, so this part of the contribution is more suggestive than actionable.

strengths: Novel and useful conceptual reframing: treating the Rashomon set itself (rather than a single deployed model) as the natural object of governance/audit, motivated by the observation that pipelines already generate multiplicity (hyperparameter sweeps, seeds, fairness constraints, etc.).

Fills a genuine gap in the literature: while fairness/interpretability within Rashomon sets are well studied, robustness, stability, and privacy interactions are comparatively underexplored, and the paper explicitly connects to and differentiates from the closest prior work (Kulynych et al. on DP multiplicity, Nguyen et al. on active learning robustness).

Reasonably broad theoretical contribution: six main theorems plus corollaries covering mutual-information bounds for sparse trees, adversarial vulnerability of single rule lists, non-transferability/reactive robustness for discrete and linear hypothesis spaces, dataset/distribution-shift stability, and a KL-divergence leakage bound for ensembles sampled from the Rashomon set, with full proofs in the appendix.

Strong integration between theory and experiments: each major theoretical claim (adversarial vulnerability-diversity relationship, stability under dataset perturbation, KL leakage growth) is paired with a matching empirical study on real datasets (COMPAS, FICO, Adult, Bank, Credit, Diabetes) using TreeFARMS-generated Rashomon sets.

The central robustness-privacy trade-off finding (Figure 1/5) is demonstrated consistently across multiple datasets and multiple tree-selection strategies (closest/farthest/increment/sparsest/densest), including sensitivity analyses in the appendix that probe robustness of the main empirical conclusion.

Clear practical framing and policy implications (internal retention vs. external disclosure of Rashomon sets, representative model disclosure) that could be useful for practitioners and regulators, going beyond a purely academic exercise.
weaknesses: The privacy analysis relies heavily on a fairly loose Chi-squared/KL bound (Theorem 6) that depends on an assumed lower bound δ on probability outputs; the bound's tightness and practical informativeness (versus, e.g., a formal differential-privacy or membership-inference guarantee) are not clearly established, and the reconstruction-error proxy used empirically (DRAFT) is specific to tree ensembles, limiting generalizability of the privacy claims to other hypothesis classes.

The adversarial robustness theory and most experiments assume a fixed, single 'optimal' model is attacked and diversity is measured relative to that one model; a more realistic adaptive adversary that targets the released Rashomon set collectively (rather than just the initially optimal model) is not analyzed, which could weaken the claimed reactive-robustness benefit in practice.

Theoretical claims for linear models (angular diversity, Theorem 3, Corollaries 1-2, and the least-squares result in Appendix B.4) are not empirically validated anywhere in the main paper or appendix — all experiments use sparse decision trees, leaving a substantial part of the theoretical contribution unverified.

Some theoretical machinery is a relatively standard application of known tools (triangle inequality, Pinsker's inequality, Chernoff/Cantelli bounds, counting arguments for entropy), so the technical novelty of individual theorems is moderate; the paper's main value is more in the framing and synthesis than in fundamentally new proof techniques.

The distinction drawn between 'distributional leakage' (Theorem 6) and 'membership privacy' (protected via Theorem 5) is asserted rather than rigorously connected — no formal argument or experiment directly quantifies membership-inference risk under Rashomon-set disclosure, so the reassurance about membership privacy remains largely qualitative.

No comparison against alternative or existing mitigation strategies (e.g., differentially private training, standard ensemble/adversarial-training robustness methods, or existing predictive-multiplicity-aware privacy mechanisms) that would help contextualize the magnitude of the trade-off or the practical value added by explicitly reasoning at the Rashomon-set level.

Presentation has some rough edges (e.g., an appendix theorem explicitly labeled 'this is not helpful' in its title, and the paper is somewhat dense with many theorem/corollary statements that could be better synthesized in the main text), and the practical 'diversity-aware disclosure policy' recommendations remain speculative without concrete algorithms or a decision procedure for selecting the amount of disclosure.

strengths: Novel and useful conceptual reframing: treats the Rashomon set itself (rather than a single deployed model) as the object of trustworthiness analysis, connecting robustness, stability, and privacy at the set level. This is a clear, well-motivated shift from prior single-model or per-property analyses (Table 1).

Solid theoretical contributions spanning multiple hypothesis spaces (decision trees/rule lists, linear models under margin-based and least-squares losses, and ensembles), with formal theorems (e.g., Thm 4.1/4.2 on single-model vulnerability, Thm 5.1-5.6 on reactive robustness, distribution-shift stability, and information leakage) and complete proofs in the appendix.

Extensive empirical validation across 6 real-world tabular datasets, several hypothesis spaces (sparse trees via TreeFARMS, linear/MLP models via AWP-based Rashomon set estimation), and even an extension to Concept Bottleneck Models on image data (AwA2), showing the qualitative robustness-privacy trade-off holds broadly.

Strong reproducibility support: detailed experimental setups, hyperparameters, datasets, and an extensive appendix (summary table of results, additional ablations on sampling strategies, sparsity effects, multi-model attacks) that would allow replication.

Practical, actionable framing for governance (reactive robustness via model rotation, disclosure sweet-spot heuristics), which is relevant to real ML deployment/auditing scenarios and moves beyond a purely academic exercise.
weaknesses: Several theoretical results rely on fairly idealized or restrictive assumptions (e.g., worst-case adversarial datasets perturbing every sample, binary features for rule-list vulnerability, exponential/margin loss for linear models, independence/bounded-correlation assumptions for ensemble theorems), so the generality claimed in the intro is only partially backed by theory; the connection to more complex architectures (MLPs, CBMs) is established empirically, not theoretically.

The gap between the theoretical privacy notion (mutual information, Theorem 4.1/5.6 in terms of KL/TV divergence) and the empirical privacy proxies used in experiments (DRAFT reconstruction error, Yeom MIA) is not formally bridged, making the theory-practice linkage somewhat loose despite qualitative alignment.

Diversity is operationalized differently across sections (Hamming distance for trees/rule lists, cosine/angular distance for linear models, pairwise correlation for ensembles) without a unifying formal definition, which slightly weakens the coherence of the central 'diversity governs the trade-off' claim.

The trade-off 'operationalization' framework in Appendix E.6-E.8 (knee-point detection, 35% tolerance threshold, privacy-constrained set size) is heuristic and somewhat arbitrary, presented without principled justification or sensitivity analysis beyond the chosen parameter.

The paper does not benchmark against established privacy-preserving baselines (e.g., differential privacy) to contextualize how severe the identified 'many near-optimal models' leakage risk is relative to standard mitigations, limiting the practical significance assessment.

The manuscript is very dense, with the bulk of technical and empirical content relegated to a lengthy appendix (39 pages total); this affects self-containedness and readability of the main text, and some figures (e.g., adversarial score vs. distance plots) are only lightly discussed.

strengths: Introduces a compelling and underexplored conceptual framing: treating the Rashomon set itself (rather than a single model) as the object of trustworthiness analysis, with a clear robustness–privacy–stability trade-off governed by model diversity.

Provides genuine theoretical breadth across multiple hypothesis classes (decision trees/rule lists via mutual information and Hamming-distance arguments, linear models via angular/margin analysis, and general bounded-loss settings for distribution-shift stability), with full proofs in the appendix that are mostly careful and correct.

Strong, extensive empirical validation: six real-world tabular datasets, five synthetic distributions, and extensions to MLPs and pretrained Concept Bottleneck Models (RashomonCBM) on AwA2, showing the qualitative trend (diversity trades off robustness vs. leakage) holds across very different model classes and attack/reconstruction methods (Kantchelian tree attacks, DRAFT reconstruction, FGSM/PGD, Yeom MIA).

Useful complementary theoretical results beyond the core trade-off: stability of the Rashomon set under small distribution shift (Thm 5.4) and dataset perturbation (Thm 5.5), and ensemble-robustness bounds (Thm C.6/C.7) that connect diversity to majority-vote robustness guarantees.

Practical operationalization discussion (Appendix E.6–E.8) translating the trade-off curves into actionable disclosure guidance (knee-point/privacy-constrained set sizes), which grounds the otherwise abstract trade-off in a governance-relevant procedure.
Thorough related-work coverage and clear positioning relative to prior Rashomon-set literature (e.g., Hsu et al. 2026 individual-model view vs. this paper's set-level view).
weaknesses: Several key theoretical results rely on fairly specific/simplified settings (binary features, single-feature-flip or L0/L2 attacks, rule lists with majority-vote leaves, i.i.d. constant-in-the-ball adversarial model) that may not transfer cleanly to richer hypothesis spaces or realistic attacker capabilities; the leap from these stylized guarantees to the general claims in the abstract/conclusion is somewhat informal.

The privacy-leakage narrative rests heavily on a single empirical proxy (DRAFT reconstruction error) and a separate MIA experiment, rather than a unified privacy measure; the MIA results (Figure 21) actually show a non-monotonic or saturating relationship with ensemble size in places, which is in some tension with the clean monotonic story emphasized in the main text.

Theorem 4.1's mutual-information bound is a loose cardinality-based bound (O(l_f log d)) that establishes a qualitative scaling but gives little quantitative insight into actual leakage, and the link between decreasing mutual information and concrete attack success (e.g., MIA advantage) is asserted via prior work rather than shown directly in this framework.

The 'reactive robustness' and disclosure-optimization framework assumes an institution can/will actively rotate models or select disclosure sizes, but does not discuss computational/operational costs of model-switching in deployment, nor does it compare against simpler baselines (e.g., standard adversarial training or ensembling) to contextualize how much the Rashomon-set approach adds.

The practical trade-off operationalization (Appendix E.6-E.8) introduces several heuristic choices (35% relative tolerance, Kneedle knee-detection, specific sampling strategies) that are presented as illustrative but are not validated against any ground-truth notion of 'safe' disclosure, limiting the rigor of the governance recommendations.

The paper is very dense, with the bulk of theoretical and empirical substance deferred to a lengthy appendix (nearly 30 pages); the main text sometimes states results without enough intuition connecting the many theorems (Thms 4.1–4.2, 5.1–5.6, C.1–C.7) into a coherent narrative, which could hinder reproducibility and accessibility for readers who do not consult the appendix.
